articles.title: Melbourne human rights activist disappears in Cambodia as wife urges Albanese government help
articles.summary:
Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese anti-human trafficking campaigner, not heard from since 18 September

The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the…

blocks.text: The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the federal government to find him and bring him home.

Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife Chloe Dang after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders.
But he never boarded his flight and has not communicated with his wife since 18 September, leaving her worried for his safety.
“My family and I are really worried about his safety, and we just only want to know where he is and what happened to him,” Dang said from Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Melbourne.
“My husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.”

Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.
The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training.

blocks.caption: Tran Hiep has not communicated with his wife since 18 September

blocks.text: Vietnam in recent years has ramped up its crackdown on dissidents, with more than 55 activists arrested under broad criminal laws in 2025.
Civil society groups and United Nations human rights experts have repeatedly warned of growing co-operation between Vietnamese authorities and neighbouring governments targeting advocates.

Viet Tan, a pro-democracy diaspora political party, has described the pair’s disappearance as concerning given previous cases involving Vietnamese dissidents vanishing in neighbouring countries and subsequently appearing in custody in Vietnam.
“Their disappearance is not an ordinary ‘missing person’ incident. Both men are long-time human rights advocates and Viet Tan members,” the organisation said.
Dang, 36, said fretting over her husband’s whereabouts had taken a psychological toll.
“It’s been 11 days and I’m really in the dark,” she said, choking back tears.
“I don’t know where he is and how he’s doing – it’s driving me crazy.
“Everything is really uncertain.”
The Australian government confirmed consular officials were in contact with Dang but declined to comment further.
“The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian reported missing in Cambodia,” a department spokesperson said on Monday.
The families of the missing men have filed an appeal with the UN working group on enforced or involuntary disappearances.

articles.title: Tennessee governor rejects clemency bid for Christa Pike as execution looms
articles.summary: If the execution proceeds, Pike would be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

blocks.text: "After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike's request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene," Governor Lee said in a statement.
Pike's legal team had filed the clemency petition earlier this month, requesting that her death sentence be commuted to life in prison.

Moving ahead with Pike's execution puts Tennessee "on singular footing", her attorneys said, as she would be the first person the state "executes in the modern death penalty era who was a teenager at the time of the offence".
Attorneys Stephen Ferrell, Kelly Gleason and Randy Spivey said the governor's decision "leaves unanswered vital questions about Tennessee's execution protocol".

"With this decision, the State of Tennessee is ignoring what both science and our legal system have decided: an 18-year-old brain is not an adult brain, and 18 is too young to face execution," they said in a statement on Monday.
The murder of Colleen Slemmer created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the 19-year-old was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest.

Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
A year later, she was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death, while then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp- who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
At the time of her incarceration, the 21-year-old was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.
Pike is scheduled to be executed on 30 September after years of failed appeals.
Colleen's mother has insisted she wants Pike's execution to move forward so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

articles.title: Obby Khan stepping down as Manitoba PC leader
articles.summary: Obby Khan is stepping down from his position as leader of Manitoba's Opposition Progressive Conservatives.

image.caption: Obby Khan speaks to reporters at the Manitoba Legislature on Monday, where he announced he was stepping down as leader of the Opposition Progressive Conservatives. (Bartley Kives/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Obby Khan is stepping down from his position as leader of Manitoba's Opposition Progressive Conservatives.
Khan was elected leader of Opposition party last year
Khan made the announcement just after 5 p.m. CT Monday, after he survived what appears to be a symbolic confidence vote on Friday.
It's not clear which member of the PC caucus triggered that vote, or for what reason.

Speaking to reporters at the legislature Monday evening, Khan said the votes in that confidence motion were two to one in his favour, but "a small group of MLAs have decided that those results are still not enough."
"It has become clear to me that after Friday's majority vote in my favour would not resolve the divisions within our caucus, it has left me no choice," Khan said.

Throughout the course of the weekend, he said he learned that some members of the PC caucus planned to meet Monday evening in what he described as an effort to "subvert the democratic will" of the caucus.
The decision to resign is "not [about] whether I could fight.… You all know me, I like to fight," said Khan.
But "I will not spend the next chapter fighting with my own party, my own caucus, when I came here to fight the NDP … and to hold this government accountable," he said.

items: Manitoba Progressive Conservative Leader Obby Khan survives caucus confidence vote

blocks.text: Khan said he will resign from the PC caucus, effective Tuesday, but will continue on as the MLA for the Winnipeg constituency of Fort Whyte, sitting as an Independent.
"I cannot be a part of a caucus with a small minority membership that lacks moral integrity, that will not abide by our rules, our principles, our code," he said.

Khan thanked some members of the 20-person PC caucus by name during his resignation speech, including former interim party leader Kelvin Goertzen, as well as MLAs Ron Schuler, Greg Nesbitt, Rick Wowchuk, Derek Johnson, Trevor King and Colleen Robbins.
'Far bigger than me'
Khan became the party leader last year, after former Manitoba Premier Heather Stefanson stepped down in early 2024.
He won the leadership in a tightly contested leadership race against Wally Daudrich, a Churchill hotel and ecotourism company owner who has since quit the party.

Khan, who was an entrepreneur and a former football player with the CFL's Winnipeg Blue Bombers before entering politics, was first elected to the Manitoba Legislature in 2022, winning the Fort Whyte seat in Winnipeg in a byelection.
He became leader in a contest sparked by the resignation of Stefanson, who stepped down as party leader months after her PCs lost the fall 2023 provincial election to Wab Kinew's NDP.
When elected to the role last year, Khan became the first Muslim, as well as the first Canadian from a South Asian ethnic background, to lead the party.

"For the first time in the party's history, someone who looked like me, prayed like me, carried a family story like mine stood here as the party leader," Khan said Monday, having to pause to collect himself as his voice cracked with emotion.
"That is far bigger than me.… Whatever happens after today remains history."

items: 'A huge honour': Obby Khan nearly moved to tears as 1st Muslim MLA in Manitoba history

blocks.text: Currently, the Tories hold 20 seats in the 57-seat Manitoba Legislature. The governing NDP have 34, the Liberals hold one and there are two Independents.
The next provincial election is not slated until October 2027.

Under the PC Party's constitution, a new leadership race can only be triggered at this point in the election cycle if the position becomes vacant, the leader ends up mentally or physically incapacitated, the leader requests a leadership race or a simple majority of PC members vote in favour of a race at a general meeting.
Manitoba's legislature is slated to resume on Tuesday.
Khan did not take questions from reporters after his nearly 20-minute speech at the legislature on Monday.
The PC Party said as of Monday evening, it did not yet know who will be serving as interim Opposition leader.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Justin Fiacconi is a journalist with CBC Manitoba, where he has worked since July 2025. A former Joan Donaldson and Peter Gzowski scholar, he has worked in two different investigative units at CBC. He graduated from Carleton University in Ottawa, Ontario, with master's degrees in journalism, and international affairs, specializing in conflict studies. His primary journalistic interest is the intersection between geopolitics and sports. He can be reached at justin.fiacconi@cbc.ca.

articles.title: RCMP confirm investigation into death threat sent to Muslim schools
articles.summary: The RCMP are among more than a half-dozen police forces probing a threat sent to Islamic schools across the country.

image.caption: The Mounties confirmed on Monday that they are investigating a hateful note sent to Islamic schools across Canada. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The RCMP are among more than a half-dozen police forces probing a threat sent to Islamic schools across the country.
More than a half-dozen police forces probing email that threatened to kill Muslims
The RCMP are among more than a half-dozen police forces probing a threat sent to Islamic schools across the country, the national police force confirmed to CBC News.

"Law enforcement agencies are working collaboratively with school leadership to investigate the reported threats and assess all available information," the RCMP said in a statement on Monday afternoon.
"We remain committed to public safety and encourage anyone with information or concerns to report them to police."
The RCMP said their northwest region is looking into the note, a division that covers the Prairie provinces as well as the Northwest Territories and Nunavut.
As of Friday, the note was sent to multiple schools in the Muslim Association of Canada's network, mostly in Ontario but also in Montreal and Vancouver.

The RCMP did not have an immediate explanation as to why the northwest region is involved in the investigation, though a section of the note, seen by CBC News, alludes to the upcoming Alberta referendum that includes a question about an eventual secession vote, stating Muslims will be "deported or slaughtered" once "Alberta becomes its own nation."

Police in Ottawa, Waterloo Region, Peel Region, London, Ont., and Montreal all told CBC News they were involved in investigations last week. Schools in their jurisdictions received the threatening note, which uses dehumanizing language against Muslims.
On Monday, Vancouver police also said in a statement they are investigating and have increased patrols across the city.
In their release, the RCMP mentioned "investigators have no information to suggest an imminent threat; however, members of the public are encouraged to remain vigilant."
Politicians condemn email
Some federal and municipal elected officials condemned the email after CBC News published the initial story on Friday, including federal Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree.

In a statement, Anandasangaree's office said the government is "deeply disturbed by the threats directed at Islamic schools and the fear they have caused students, families, educators and Muslim communities across Canada," adding "Canadians must stand together against Islamophobia and all forms of hate."
Liberal MP Iqra Khalid said she is appalled by the threats.
"Two of my own nieces attend one of the schools that received threatening messages," she said in a statement.
The MP for Mississauga-Erin Mills said the threats must be taken seriously and "those responsible must be held accountable."
Mississauga Mayor Carolyn Parrish called the threats "incredibly disturbing," and said threatening children is "especially despicable."
Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe also said he is "deeply troubled" by the messages.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Raffy Boudjikanian is a senior reporter with the CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa. He has also worked in Edmonton, Calgary and Montreal for the public broadcaster.

articles.title: Investigation of alleged gang-rape at Cornell University fraternity house reopened
articles.summary: Outrage over treatment of alleged offenders, members of Chi Phi fraternity, has grown since lawsuit was made public

blocks.text: Prosecutors in New York said on Monday that they have reopened an investigation into the alleged gang-rape of a student at Cornell University after an outcry over “leniency” shown to seven fraternity members named as the perpetrators.

According to lawyers for the student, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours.
None of the seven were arrested, they said, and the others were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions.

On Monday, Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, said his office was looking again at the case, after the woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago.
Later on Monday, Van Houten released a fuller statement defending his office’s past decision to not seek charges.

“While I generally refrain from commenting publicly on criminal investigations, the community outrage stemming from the incomplete news and social media coverage requires that I provide an answer to why the investigation resulted in a lack of criminal charges,” he said.

He went on to say: “Jane Doe’s sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later.

“Furthermore, I have never been contacted by Jane Doe’s attorneys. Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision. Rather, I reached out to Jane Doe’s attorneys after the lawsuit was filed to understand the discrepancy between the original statement and the lawsuit’s allegations and the proper path forward in light of the lawsuit’s allegations,” Van Houten continued.

The district attorney said that he has asked a senior female prosecutor to prepare a case for a grand jury, adding that he “recogniz[es] that the process of healing from trauma is personal and different for every human”.
“Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” he said.
Van Houten also released a summary of a “six-page, single-spaced, typewritten statement” that Doe provided to the Cornell University police department in November 2024.

According to the summary, Doe told police that she agreed to engage in sexual activity with two Chi Phi members, “due to how attracted [she] was to [Male Number 1 ] on top of [her] drunken curiousness”.

“When she learned that Male Number 2 would be the third participant, Jane Doe ‘remembered being excited because [she] thought that [Male Number 1 and Male Number 2] wanting to have a threesome meant that they were gay’,” the summary said.
The summary added that another man entered the room and shook Doe’s hand.

“When [Jane Doe] made contact with [Male Number 3’s] hand, [Male Number 3] pulled [Jane Doe] into him and [they] began making out. While [Male Number 3] was kissing [her], [Male Number 2] began groping [her]. Eventually, ‘[Male Number 2, Male Number 3, and Jane Doe] would end up on the bed next to where [Male Number 1] was sleeping and [they] began to have a threesome,’” according to the summary, which said that four men later entered the room.

“Jane Doe had difficulty remembering parts of what happened next. She remembered ‘[Male Number 7] said something very rude and mean to [her].’ Male Number 7 apologized and ‘grabbed [her] face and started kissing [her]’. Jane Doe ‘quickly backed away to stop [Male Number 7] from kissing [her]’,” the summary said.
It went on to say that some of the Chi Phi members started to compliment Doe’s looks and asked if they could take drugs off her body.

“Jane Doe responded, ‘Sure.’ While the men were doing drugs off of her body, ‘[Male Number 3] and [another male] entered the room and said something like, ‘Ok we’re shutting down whatever the f*** this is,’” the summary added.

Outrage over the treatment of the alleged offenders has grown since the lawsuit was made public. The woman, who quit the university afterwards, said she went to visit a friend at the Chi Phi frat house in an already intoxicated state.
“When plaintiff arrived at Xi chapter’s fraternity house, plaintiff was visibly intoxicated as she had consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past 3 hours,” Doe’s lawsuit said.

According to the lawsuit, one of the defendants “pulled [her] off to a quieter area and propositioned her with having a threesome with her and another one of his fraternity brothers. In her drunken state, plaintiff was incapable of consenting to this proposition.”

The lawsuit then alleges that two men “pressured plaintiff into snorting the alleged Ketamine with them, a drug she had never done before. During this time, [the two men] also plied plaintiff with marijuana and ‘Jamaican Liquor’ believed to be some type of high-proof rum.”
While they sexually assaulted her, she alleges, a message was sent to a frat house Snapchat group called Chi Phi Actives that stated there was “free pussy upstairs”.
At least five other frat members showed up and joined in, she said, and her ordeal lasted until about 5.45am “and plaintiff lost consciousness”, the lawsuit said.

It also alleges that Doe was “slapped” multiple times and that her “phone was on the other side of the room and she felt as if there was no way for her to escape this room full of predatory, fraternity men”.

“When plaintiff awoke later that day, on October 20, 2024, plaintiff returned to her residence within the Alpha Beta chapter sorority house. At this point, plaintiff was in a state of shock. At her residence, plaintiff noticed a large bruise that had formed on her buttocks and took pre-emptive medication for a urinary tract infection,” the lawsuit said.
She made a report to campus police about three weeks later.

Cornell’s vice-president for university relations, Kyle Kimball, issued a statement on 21 September calling the allegations “deeply disturbing”. Kimball’s statement claimed the Ivy League institution’s offices of civil rights, student conduct and community standards carried out a number of inquiries at the time.

Following the district attorney’s decision to reopen the case on Monday, Kimball said: “Cornell University supports the decision of the Tompkins County District Attorney (DA) to provide an opportunity for the victim’s story in the 2024 Chi Phi fraternity sexual assault case to be heard by a criminal grand jury.”
Kimball added that the “involved fraternity chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus”.

An attorney for the student told CBS News that none of the alleged perpetrators faced legal consequences for their conduct, and nobody in the frat house that saw the message did anything to stop the rapes from taking place.
“Not one of these guys was arrested,” said the lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. “Not one. That I can tell you for a fact.
“There were so many people that could have prevented it and they didn’t. I’ve never seen anything like it.”
Giuffra also countered the statement of Van Houten, the Tompkins district attorney, which lays out what he said the alleged victim stated in her original police complaint from November 2024.
“She never says that she was drugged without her knowledge,” Van Houten said.

“She admits to taking drugs and alcohol voluntarily and with knowledge. She does not allege that she was forced to engage in any acts. She does not say that she was physically helpless or unconscious or incapacitated at any point during the time at the fraternity house.”
Giuffra told ABC News that neither the district attorney or Cornell police ever followed up with his client.
“In my experience, speaking with an abuse survivor requires delicacy, understanding and specialized training,” he said.

“An average university police officer would not have these skills. It would be the role of a specially trained detective or district attorney. However, Ms Doe was never contacted by anybody with those skills.”

Giuffra also said: “My client went to the Cornell University police because a crime was committed. It was the obligation of the police to investigate the complaints. They were given the group chat inviting the members of the fraternity to rape my client.

“This was a critical piece of evidence supporting that a crime had occurred. Despite this there was no follow-up with Ms Doe either by the Cornell police or the Tompkins county district attorney,” he added.
Named defendants in the lawsuit are Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar.
Two of those defendants denied the allegations in statements to ABC News.
“At bottom, Scott never sexually assaulted or even touched the plaintiff in any way,” Jeremy Saland, an attorney for Kretzschmar, said. “Period.”
Norris denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use – but acknowledged he sent a message that was included in the complaint.
“I thoughtlessly engaged in Snapchat and briefly stopped in the room where misconduct happened but not when it happened,” he said.
On Sunday, the Academy Award-nominated actor Florence Pugh posted a lengthy statement on Instagram about Giuffra’s client, praising the “unbelievably powerful” victim and her “strong will”.

“This is really the moment where we need our men to be as horrified and as sickened as us,” Pugh wrote. “You need to be leading conversations about how we change the allowance and complicity of this behaviour as much as we are.”

In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title: Ukraine hit with deadly wave of Russian drone strikes in Kyiv and across the country
articles.summary: At least two people were killed when a drone hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv on Monday, as Russia pounded the heart of the Ukrainian capital with some of the most persistent…

image.caption: Flames are seen at Kyiv's Dobrobut Hospital on Monday in the aftermath of a Russian drone strike. (Evgeniy Maloletka/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

At least two people were killed when a drone hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv on Monday, as Russia pounded the heart of the Ukrainian capital with some of the most persistent drone strikes since the start of the war.
Ukraine's Zelenskyy says majority of Russian drones were jet-powered
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said nine people had been killed and more than 80 injured in Russian drone strikes throughout the country.

Two people were killed in the assault on the Academy of Sciences building in the ​heart of the capital. Emergency services said later in the evening that one of the dead ​had been recovered from under rubble.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 24 people had been injured in several attacks on the capital, six of whom were being treated in hospital.
Sirens echoed through the streets as smoke billowed into the sky and air raids sounded late into the day.
In ​recent weeks, Russia has begun hitting Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with faster, high-flying jet drones.
Struggle to defend against jet drones

In his nightly video address, Zelenskyy said ⁠Ukraine was still having difficulty countering faster, high-flying ⁠Russian jet-powered drones — 90 of 120 drones fired on Ukraine were jet propelled, rather than propeller-driven, ‌and the interception rate was 57 per cent.

"New interceptors are being actively tested," he said. "Some combat groups are using them, but, of course, some details still need to be refined to achieve enough effectiveness and scale. We are speeding up the developers."

Officials had noted attacks on other targets, including a pharmaceutical company, petrol stations and a medical facility in Kyiv. In other cities and regions, civilian facilities, businesses and communications infrastructure were targeted.
Zelenskyy also detailed a report from Ukraine's Main Directorate ⁠of Intelligence (HUR) which he said showed that Russia had launched a new wave of mobilization for its military.

"They are increasing the number of people they recruit through various methods," he said. "It is important that the governments of countries from which Russia recruits people for its army take action against this."
People climb out windows to escape burning Kyiv academy after Russian drone strike
Zelenskyy said 8,000 North Korean troops, first brought to Russia in 2024 to counter ‌a Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region, remained in the country and a further 10,000 were being trained.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed as "utter nonsense" any notion that Moscow is ordering a new mobilization.
Deaths in Dnipro, Synelnykove
In the southeastern city of Dnipro, a Russian drone attack on the business centre killed three, officials said.
In particular, Russia has been widening its attacks on economic targets beyond warehouses, port facilities and energy infrastructure, in recent days hitting data ​centres and telecoms facilities.

items: Why is it so difficult for Ukraine to take down Russia's jet-powered drones?

blocks.text: Another person was killed in a logistics office in Synelnykove, southeast of Dnipro, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Emergency services said an attack on infrastructure in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured 32 people.

In Kyiv, flames leaped from ⁠the opened interior of the historic Academy building, and rubble was strewn across the courtyard, partially burying one car. Firefighters doused the building in water and searched for people ⁠in the wreckage, while two survivors of the blast clambered from upper story windows, onto ladders raised by emergency services.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia of cynicism for targeting ⁠a scientific ⁠institution during the working day.

"Russia is deliberately expanding the boundaries ​of what it believes the world will tolerate. Every attack left without a strong response only encourages the next one," he said, calling on Ukraine's allies to provide it with more ​air defences.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said 19 people ⁠had been injured in the daytime attack on the business centre in Dnipro.
Hanzha said the centre was surrounded by residential buildings, a park, a library and offices in the city centre: "Hundreds of people are here in the middle of the working day."
24 hours in Kyiv: Living through Russian drone strikes
Ukraine has also increased attacks on Russia, targeting oil refineries as well as online retailers to try to undermine revenues and support for Moscow's war effort.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that it had struck Russian oil facilities in the Krasnodar region and two defence plants.
Both sides have denied deliberately targeting civilians.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The two countries have been in a state of all-out war ever since.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: What to know about Cornell's alleged frat house gang-rape case and the 'Cornell 7'
articles.summary: Investigators in New York are reopening an investigation into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University after a woman filed a lawsuit claiming the university didn't do enough to protect her.

image.caption: A student walks past a Cornell University sign in Ithaca, N.Y., Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (Heather Ainsworth/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it. It also contains vulgar language.

Alumni are threatening to pull funding, celebrities are lashing out and people are boycotting institutions associated with an alleged gang rape at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., currently igniting the internet.

The case came into the spotlight after the victim, known only as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging the private Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed "the Cornell 7." She claims they drugged and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024.

The lawsuit, filed in New York Supreme Court and viewed by CBC News, alleges the assault happened on campus at the Chi Phi Fraternity house, and that one of the frat brothers sent a Snapchat message inviting other members to join them for "free pussy."
It further claims that the accused only faced temporary suspensions and "were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays" to the university — a claim Cornell denies.

None of the fraternity members have been criminally charged. But the case has unleashed online fury, drawing comparisons to last year's Hockey Canada sexual assault trial in London, Ont., which saw all five players acquitted.
On Monday, the Tompkins County district attorney announced he was reopening the investigation.

"Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available — by testimony to the Tompkins County grand jury," district attorney Matthew Van Houten told CBC News in a written statement.

Cornell, in its own statement Monday, said it supported the DA's decision for a criminal grand jury to hear the woman's claims, but disputed the lawsuit's allegations about how the university punished the accused.
"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Kyle Kimball, vice-president for university relations, said in a statement posted online.
The statement also said the on-campus Chi Phi chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.
Here's what to know about the case and why it's caused so much fury online.
What's in the lawsuit?

According to the lawsuit, the assault began the night of Oct. 19, 2024. Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time, had been drinking with her sorority, and again at a nightclub and then "stumbled" alone at 11 p.m. to the Chi Phi fraternity house on campus to visit a friend — one of the accused.

"Plaintiff was visibly intoxicated as she had consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past three hours," the lawsuit says. It also says the nightclub served the woman "at least one" alcoholic beverage even though it had marked an X on her hand showing she was underage.
At the frat house, she was given a beer, and her friend allegedly proposed a threesome with another member, to which she was too intoxicated to consent, the suit states.

The accused allegedly took her upstairs and led her to a room with another of the accused. She was pressured to snort ketamine, the lawsuit alleges, adding that she had never used that substance before. They also "plied her" with cannabis and rum, it says, after which the two men "began engaging in sexual acts with plaintiff, all without her consent."

items: Hockey Canada sexual assault trial 'reinvigorated' talk on complex issues of consent, sports culture
Intense backlash in Edmonton greets Oilers signing of Alex Formenton

blocks.text: As they engaged in oral and vaginal sex, one of the accused also repeatedly slapped her buttocks, resulting in bruising, the lawsuit says. One of the men left to have a nap, and another entered the room. The two remaining men then began another alleged assault on the woman.

At 1:42 a.m., one of them sent a Snapchat message to the rest of the fraternity, claiming there was "free pussy." The suit includes an image of the alleged message, and some of the purported responses from the accused, including, "like you can walk in and whip it out."
Text messages and consent at the Hockey Canada sex assault trial

According to the suit, "multiple" other fraternity members then entered the room. One of them allegedly put ketamine on his erect penis and told the woman to snort it, which she did. The men then began snorting the substance off her naked body, the suit states. Two men took her to another room, where they allegedly assaulted her again.

The alleged incident ended at 5:45 a.m., and Jane Doe passed out. She returned to her sorority house "in a state of shock," the documents state, and soon realized the events were becoming "public knowledge" on campus.

She reported it a few weeks later to the Cornell University Police Department around Nov. 8, 2024. She alleges the seven accused were issued temporary suspensions and allowed "to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays."
The university released a statement and investigated, but ultimately closed it at a later date, according to the lawsuit.

Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the alleged assault and the university's purported handling of it, the lawsuit says. She is suing the seven men, the Chi Phi fraternity, the university, Moonies Bar and Nightclub and others, seeking undisclosed damages.
The seven Chi Phi members named in the lawsuit are Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar.
"Ms. Doe has had her dreams destroyed as a result of what has happened to her," her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told CBC News in a written statement.
"The fact that her trauma has been made public has been very difficult. However, she has been gratified by the outpouring of support that she has received from the public."
Online backlash to 'the culture of rape'

As the lawsuit made headlines, the backlash was swift. Online, Cornell alumni called on each other to stop donating to the school. Some people publicly turned down their acceptances, and others launched campaigns targeting the university, the local police and the various workplaces of the so-called "Cornell 7."
The seven accused were outed by Cornell's student newspaper editorial board on Sept. 21 in an editorial titled, "Cornell won't, we will."

A former South Park writer launched a website to expose the accused. Actors Josh Gad and Florence Pugh posted online condemning the alleged assault and what the lawsuit described as the university's handling of it.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned what she called a "culture of rape" at elite institutions while speaking about the alleged incident, at a town hall in Ithaca over the weekend.
"This is a culture, this is norms, these are practices," said Ocasio-Cortez, according to the Cornell Daily Sun. “What we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore.”
Cornell's response
The university said in a statement Monday that it conducted its own investigation at the time and issued sanctions, including expelling some students and suspending others.
In response to the claims, Cornell said "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."

The school said it conducted an internal disciplinary investigation in 2024. It said a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days, and both the woman and the accused testified and presented evidence.
In a statement last week responding to the lawsuit, Cornell said federal privacy law barred it from disclosing specific information on individual students.
Reopening the case

Van Houten, the district attorney, said Monday that in light of the attention the case has received, he wanted to clarify why the original investigation did not result in criminal charges. He said that Jane Doe went to campus police at the time, but did not, in her initial sworn statement, make any claims of being gang-raped or drugged.
"On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual," he said.
The prosecutor also said the woman's attorney did not contact him about her statement or about reconsidering the decision not to prosecute.
'She was traumatized'
Giuffra, Jane Doe's lawyer, defended his client while blaming the university police investigation.
"In the days following the assault, she was traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode," Giuffra told CBC News.
He questioned why she wasn't contacted by the DA's office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors.

items: Interactive: Campus sexual assault reports
Ryerson, Acadia University statements on CBC's campus sexual assaults report

blocks.text: "It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she ... never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint," Giuffra added.

Multiple media now report that the seven accused men have sought legal representation. CBC News has reached out to Jeremy Saland, one of the lawyers identified, and has not yet heard back. But Saland told BBC his client denies the allegations.

His client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat," but "did nothing else," the outlet reported. Saland said his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine."

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​

articles.title: French PM warns against escalation of school protests after 164 arrested
articles.summary: Students are protesting over issues such as overcrowded classes, but the prime minister has condemned reports of violence.

blocks.text: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has warned that any escalation in the country's current wave of student protests would be "irresponsible", following the arrests of 164 people on Monday.
The demonstrations, which started in Paris and have seen teenagers blockading their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages.
Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."
But a French union that defends the interests of high school students said the protests were a "legitimate response" to the conditions they face.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 12 members of the security forces, 12 students and three school staff were injured on Monday, while 180 schools were affected.
He did not provide further details on those who had been arrested.
The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris.
Incidents of vandalism were reported, along with fireworks being aimed at police, and the protests have now spread to other regions in France.

According to the AFP news agency, four high schools were reportedly blockaded in the southern regions of Alpes-Maritimes and Var. Protests have also been reported in Marseille, the northern Lille area and Sedan in the north-eastern Ardennes.
The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, defended the protests in a post on social media.

"Lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classes, stress caused by Parcoursup [the web platform used in France for students to apply to the first year of higher education]... These issues are by no means inevitable, but simply the result of 10 years of Macron's policies and the lack of resources in the national education system," it said.
It called on students to blockade schools on Tuesday in defence of "their rights and against budget austerity".
On the same day, unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants also called for a day of walkouts to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions.

In response to the student movement, Lecornu said "the difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed", but that "violence must be condemned unequivocally, and its perpetrators must answer for their actions".
The prime minister also accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of urging students to expand the movement.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, LFI's leader, blamed the Lecornu government for having "ordered the crackdown" on the protest, adding that the high school students taking part were "harmless".
But Nuñez said the demonstrations and blockades were "not very typical protest movements".

"It is much more like urban violence, with a number of individuals who were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes, equipped with projectiles, who clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces," he said.
"It wasn't about making demands; it was really violence in its purest form."
Since the protests began, several incidents involving violence between students and police officers have been reported.
In one incident, a police officer reportedly fired a round from a grenade launcher used for crowd control, injuring a high school student, according to France's BFMTV.
Investigations have been launched into these incidents, the broadcaster added.

articles.title: Alberta youth charged with terrorism offences related to violent online group 764
articles.summary: RCMP have charged a 17-year-old in Lethbridge, Alta., with multiple offences related to terrorism, child sexual abuse and exploitation material, and animal cruelty. The accused’s online activity was…

image.caption: 764 is a network of online predators that targets children and coerces them into acts of self-harm and violence. In 2025, Canada was the first country to designate the group as terrorists. (CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

RCMP have charged a 17-year-old in Lethbridge, Alta., with multiple offences related to terrorism, child sexual abuse and exploitation material, and animal cruelty. The accused’s online activity was consistent with the designated terrorist group 764, investigators say.
Group described as transnational network of online predators targeting vulnerable youths
RCMP have charged a 17-year-old in Lethbridge, Alta., with multiple offences and say the teen's online activity was consistent with the designated terrorist group 764.

The group is a transnational network of online predators targeting vulnerable youths with the goal of coercing victims to commit acts of self-harm as well as violence and abuse against others and animals, according to police.

The RCMP Federal Policing Northwest Region’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team (INSET) says it received information from the Lethbridge police, which led to the arrest. The teen faces charges related to terrorism, child sexual abuse and exploitation material, and animal cruelty.
CBC’s the fifth estate previously reported on 764, describing how the group targets victims online through platforms like Telegram, Discord, Roblox, TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, Twitch and Steam.
Trapped: The Online Terror Network

Once targeted, victims are coerced into providing sexually explicit images of themselves and into committing acts of self-harm or violence against animals, often on livestreams. The predators exert further control by threatening to release the images to the victim's friends, family or school.

As the abuse escalates, some victims are forced into abusing others or attempting to take their own life, and at least one school shooting in the United States has been linked to 764, according to reporting by the fifth estate.
The RCMP provides a resource sheet for parents and guardians about these online groups, signs of online extortion or abuse, and where to find help.

items: Q&A: Here's how an RCMP officer says you can help protect children from online extortion

blocks.text: The RCMP says that 764 is one of several groups engaging in similar activity, which are collectively referred to as the COM (short for community). In 2025, Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.
The Lethbridge teenager is set to appear in court Oct. 14.
The accused cannot be named in accordance with the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

articles.title: Retired Yukon teacher in Florida to see former student Joshua Kutryk launch into space
articles.summary: Kutryk, who is heading to the International Space Station later this week, has credited Ted Hupé, his former Grade 6 teacher in Yukon, with inspiring "the explorer within me."

image.caption: Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk holds up his fingers to make the number 13 to mark his launch as part of Crew 13 launch to the International Space Station. Kutryk and three other astronauts are set to launch on Oct. 1. (SpaceX)

blocks.text: North·New
Kutryk, who is heading to the International Space Station later this week, has credited Ted Hupé, his former Grade 6 teacher in Yukon, with inspiring "the explorer within me."
Kutryk has credited his former teacher Ted Hupé with inspiring 'the explorer within me'
When Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk leaves Earth later this week to journey to the International Space Station, one of his former teachers from the Yukon will have a front-row seat.

"To be invited to go and be in close proximity to the launch, everyone here says that's a pretty special thing to have a chance to go and see," said Ted Hupé on Monday morning from Cape Canaveral, Fla.
Kutryk will be riding on SpaceX's Crew Dragon to the International Space Station, where he'll be living and working for roughly six months.

Hupé, now retired, was Kutryk's Grade 6 teacher at Christ the King Elementary School in Whitehorse, and he and his wife received a special invitation to go watch the launch on Thursday. The invite came in recognition of the impact Hupé had on his former student, decades ago.
Kutryk was born in Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., and lived in Whitehorse for five years as a child.

Speaking to CBC News in 2017, when he was chosen by the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) in its recruitment program, Kutryk described how he had been inspired as a young man by Hupé's world travels, including treks in Nepal, and cycling trips in New Zealand and India.
"To me as a Grade 6 child, that was one of the things that ignited this exploratory sense, the explorer within me, that has really been there for the whole ride," Kutryk said.
"He [Hupé] left a life-lasting impact."
Hupé calls that sort of appreciation "humbling."
"Like, I had no idea that the stories I told and the interactions that I had with Josh and his particular class would have a lasting impact.
"You just have no idea some of the things you say or do will leave that lasting impression — so you've got to be careful!" Hupé said with a laugh.
He remembers Kutryk as a "pretty studious kid," quiet, serious — and extremely competitive.
"He was just a great kid," Hupé said. "Josh was one of those kids who wanted to excel in everything that he did."

Hupé and his wife have a lot on their agenda this week in Florida. They'll tour the Kennedy Space Centre, and on Tuesday they'll get to see and wave to Kutryk and the other quarantined astronauts, "at a distance that allows us not to infect them with a cold or the flu or anything."
Then, they'll be there for the launch on Thursday morning, and afterwards attend a reception hosted by the Canadian Space Agency.
The Crew 13 launch, as it's called, will also include NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.
The crew will join several astronauts who are already on station and will conduct several experiments, some of which are Canadian.
Hupé says seeing his former student "literally reach for the stars" is incredible.
"As a longtime teacher, you always want your kids to do well," he said. "I'm just humbled to think that something I did actually made a difference."
With files from TJ Dhir and Nicole Mortillaro

articles.title: New York Times executive fatally shot allegedly by elderly in-laws
articles.summary: Jonathan McKinsey's in-laws, who are both 77 years old, face multiple charges including first-degree murder.

blocks.text: A New York Times executive was fatally shot in California, allegedly by his wife's elderly parents who have been arrested on suspicion of murder.

Jonathan McKinsey, 40, the newspaper's director of engineering for games player experience, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in a car park in Dublin - 35 miles (56km) west of San Francisco - on Saturday afternoon, police said.
Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, his parents-in-law who are both 77 years old, are facing multiple charges, including first-degree murder.
It was unclear whether the couple have a lawyer, and they are due to appear in court to formally face the charges on Wednesday.
McKinsey's death was confirmed by The New York Times.
His body was found at 15:00 (23:00 GMT) on Thursday afternoon outside the Dublin Sports Grounds.
Witnesses told KGO-TV in San Francisco that they heard a flurry of gunshots, before seeing the victim on the ground.
"I saw the guy drop to the floor: head bloody and chest bloody," witness Assad Razawi told the news outlet.
His daughter added that her father saw the couple "walking together and then casually walk away from the shooting".
The couple were arrested several minutes later by an officer passing by the scene. They had remained in the area after the attack, a witness said.
McKinsey was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police.
Police have not disclosed any motive for his killing.
The elderly couple are being held at the Santa Rita jail.
They also face charges of felony conspiracy, wilful discharge of a firearm with gross negligence, and child endangerment.

articles.title: Australia news live: Chalmers defends record as RBA’s cash rate decision due
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

blocks.text: Key events

items: 23m agoWelcome

blocks.text: There were 30 drowning deaths in 2025-2026, the highest number in almost a decade, according to a Royal Life Saving Australia report that Australian Associated Press reports on.
Of them, 14 involved more than one death, often related to boating, driving through floodwater, or people exploring unfamiliar environments, chief executive Justin Scarr said.
double quotation markThe message is to know the swimming skills of all the people in your group.
It is the largest spike in deaths since 2016-2017, when 34 lives were lost.
Over the past decade there have been with 229 deaths, or an average of 23 per year.
In the most recent year, 83% of drowning victims were men, 37% were born overseas and a quarter were aged between 65 and 74.
Nearly one-third of the fatal events were related to boating, while driving through floodwater and swimming were the other leading circumstances.
Besides the RBA decison at 2.30pm, the other big political story of the day is that Larissa Waters is standing down as Greens leader.
She said last night that a kidney disease she has been managing has recently worsened and that she needs to stand down.
Here’s our story from political editor Tom McIlroy:

blocks.caption: Catie McLeod

blocks.text: Catie McLeod

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has defended his economic record on the eve of what is widely expected to be the fourth interest rate rise of 2026, as the Reserve Bank remains concerned about persistent inflation.
The RBA board is poised to hike the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% on Tuesday, which would be the fourth increase in 2026 and push typical home loan interest rates to 6.5%.

Speaking on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night, Chalmers emphasised the factors contributing to inflation, saying that Australia was performing well considering what was going on in the world, particularly in the Middle East.

double quotation markWe have a lot going for us and we’ve got a lot of work to do to make sure that in these difficult global circumstances Australia continues to out-perform the world. We have a big inflation challenge in our economy. It’s made much worse by decisions taken on the other side of the world. From an economic point of view this war in Iran has been an absolute disaster for Australian families, because they have been asked to pay a hefty price.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.

Jim Chalmers has defended his stewardship of the economy ahead of what is widely expected to be the fourth interest rate rise of 2026 as the Reserve Bank tries to bring down persistent inflation. More coming up.

Besides the RBA decision at 2.30pm, the other big political story of the day is that Larissa Waters is standing down as Greens leader. We’ll have reaction as it comes in this morning plus the latest on who might replace her.

articles.title: Canada did not see historic population decline last year, StatsCan says after second look
articles.summary: Canada's population saw a slight bump in 2025, Statistics Canada says, revising a previous estimate that showed the population decreased for the first time in the country's history.

image.caption: Canada's population saw an increase of 280,810 last year, according to revised federal data. (Brian Morris/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Canada's population saw a slight bump in 2025, Statistics Canada says, revising a previous estimate that showed the population decreased for the first time in the country's history.
Preliminary numbers suggested population decreased for first time in Canada's history
The statistics agency released new numbers last week that suggest the population grew slightly, by 280,810 people, in all of 2025.
The new estimate is a revision from data released in March that indicated the country had seen an annual net decline in residents for the first time since Confederation.

"These estimates were preliminary and Statistics Canada indicated at the time that upcoming updates could be larger than usual and that the estimated population decrease could become an increase as more complete administrative data became available," a Statistics Canada spokesperson said in an email.
The agency said in March that the initial estimate should be treated "with caution" because work and study permit extensions could "lead to larger than usual updates" in the future.
Growth still slow, StatsCan says
The agency said the revised estimate still indicates a significant slowdown in population growth.
The government under former prime minister Justin Trudeau began cutting back on both permanent and temporary immigration after it rapidly increased during the post-pandemic labour shortage.
Prior to Prime Minister Mark Carney taking office, the Liberals had already taken steps to shrink temporary residents' share of Canada's population.
Carney's first budget said Canada would admit only 385,000 temporary residents in 2026 — about 43 per cent fewer than the 2025 target — and 370,000 in 2027 and 2028.
The budget also said that the federal government would limit the number of new permanent residents to 380,000 annually between 2026 and 2028.

articles.title: Dutch police arrest security professional in ShinyHunters investigation
articles.summary: A Dutch man whose journey from cybercriminal to reformed security professional was widely covered in the international media has been arrested ‌as part of an investigation into the hacker group…

image.caption: Dutch police have arrested a man as part of an investigation into hacking group ShinyHunters. (Kacper Pempel/Illustration/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A Dutch man whose journey from cybercriminal to reformed security professional was widely covered in the international media has been arrested ‌as part of an investigation into the hacker group ShinyHunters, Dutch police and the man's boss said on Monday. The news comes on the heels of ShinyHunters hacking the FBI last week.
The arrest of the 24-year-old 'reformed hacker' left his boss 'flabbergasted'

A Dutch man whose journey from cybercriminal to reformed security professional was widely covered in the international media has been arrested ‌as part of an investigation into the hacker group ShinyHunters, Dutch police and the man's boss said on Monday.
In a statement posted to the social media site X, Dutch police said that a ​24-year-old man had been arrested in connection with the ​inquiry and would appear in court in Rotterdam on Tuesday.

The statement did not identify the man by name, but ​his boss, Benjamin Korper of Amsterdam-based cybersecurity company Neo Security, said it ⁠was Pepijn van ⁠der Stap, the company's offensive security ‌lead.
In a telephone interview with Reuters, Korper said his office was visited by Dutch forensic investigators on Sept. 15, the same night Van der Stap was arrested in a police raid.

Van der Stap's ⁠2023 convictions on data theft and extortion charges received widespread publicity, as did his subsequent disavowal of cybercrime. Korper said he had carefully vetted Van der Stap before hiring him ‌and was shocked by the arrest.
"Absolutely everybody I talked to is flabbergasted,” he said.

items: What drives ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for hacking the FBI?
FBI employee data allegedly hacked by ShinyHunters contains sensitive info about intelligence roles

blocks.text: He said he had hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, ​but so far investigators have found no evidence that he acted against his employer or its clients.
Korper ⁠said he had not been in touch with Van der Stap since the ⁠arrest. Attempts by Reuters to reach Van der Stap or identify a ⁠lawyer ⁠or representative were not immediately successful.
News ​of Van der Stap's arrest was first reported by independent journalist Brian Krebs.

ShinyHunters ​is a hacking group ⁠known for large-scale data thefts and extortion, most notable of late for the alleged hack of the FBI, where it boasted of stealing a large amount of data about current and former FBI employees.

articles.title: TikTok, X reportedly barring ads for documentary about Elon Musk
articles.summary: Ads for a documentary about controversial billionaire Elon Musk have reportedly been banned from both TikTok and X but, after brief delays, are now running on YouTube and Meta's social media…

image.caption: Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, attends the Viva Technology conference in Paris, on June 16, 2023. (Gonzalo Fuentes/File Photo/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Ads for a documentary about controversial billionaire Elon Musk have reportedly been banned from both TikTok and X but, after brief delays, are now running on YouTube and Meta's social media platforms.
YouTube, Meta say ads for Musk now running after brief delays

Ads for a documentary putting a critical lens on controversial billionaire Elon Musk have reportedly been banned from both TikTok and X but, after brief delays, are now running on YouTube and Meta's social media platforms.
The trailer for the nearly four-hour film Musk dropped on Thursday ahead of its Oct. 9 theatrical release.

But on Friday, a story in the Hollywood Reporter said indie distributor Bleecker Street was rejected by all four companies when it attempted to buy ads on the platforms for the film. YouTube, TikTok and Meta — parent company to Facebook and Instagram — reportedly blamed its "political content" while X, which Musk owns, did not comment.
In the wake of an online backlash, YouTube said on Saturday that ads for Musk are now running on the platform.
"When submitted as an ad, it was temporarily restricted by our system," YouTube said through its updates account on X. "Following review the ad has been cleared to run."
A spokesperson for Meta told CBC News on Monday that the ads "were rejected in error and have been restored," without elaborating.
Bleecker Street, TikTok and X did not return calls for comment.

TikTok does not permit paid political ads, and Meta restricts them in some regions such as the European Union. YouTube allows political ads with transparency disclosures, and X permits them in regions including the U.S.

Musk's political profile rose sharply when he campaigned for U.S. President Donald Trump's re-election in 2024 and ultimately joined his administration as head of the budget-slashing Department of Government Efficiency. He has since left the administration, but remains a divisive and outspoken figure.
But while Musk's trailer includes brief clips from his appearances on the campaign trail, it's unclear how this would qualify it as the type of campaign ads covered by platforms' restrictions.

One of the topics of the film is how the richest man in the world has allegedly aimed to control conversation online — digging into his purchase of Twitter, now X, and allegations that Musk, despite his free-speech stylings, may have used his Starlink satellites to improperly influence the 2024 election.
'Censorious platforms'
After YouTube and Meta said they had OK'd the ads, director Alex Gibney said the "public pressure worked."
"The censorious platforms backed down,” he wrote Saturday on X.

Gibney later posted a 2022 quote from a Musk press release about his acquisition of Twitter, in which he stated "free speech is the bedrock of a functioning democracy, and Twitter is the digital town square where matters vital to the future of humanity are debated."
"Will X allow ads for the trailer for my film 'Musk,' about the self-proclaimed 'free-speech absolutist?'" he wrote.
Since 2023, when Gibney announced his intent to make the film, Musk has consistently called it a "hit piece."

He called Gibney "a horrible human" and "a bitter old man who lost the plot long ago" on X in the wake of the film’s debut at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month. He also reportedly threatened the production with legal action over its insinuations about the Starlink satellites.
The film has been widely praised by critics.

items: Justice Department under Trump asks EU to scrap $137M US fine for Elon Musk's X
Elon Musk calls documentary about him a 'hit piece' after buzzy debut
Tesla being investigated after car drives into home, killing 76-year-old woman

blocks.text: Vulture, the arts wing of New York magazine, called it a “damning” portrayal of Musk that left the reviewer “terrified at how much money and power he’s accrued,” while the trade paper Variety called it a "lacerating portrait of technocratic brilliance, power lust and crackpot delusion."

Musk isn't the only tech billionaire coming under the camera this year. Aaron Sorkin's dramatized The Social Reckoning, a followup to 2010's The Social Network, which Sorkin wrote, which puts the spotlight on Mark Zuckerberg, will be released by Sony next month.
Elon Musk could become world's 1st trillionaire with SpaceX IPO
