articles.title: US sanctions on Iran's aviation industry make travel less predictable as countries cancel flights
articles.summary: The threat of secondary US sanctions is putting pressure on airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies that service Iranian airlines. Some countries have already canceled flights.

image.caption: Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the IRGC [FILE: JUNE 2022]Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: US sanctions are pushing Iran's weakened aviation sector toward deeper isolation, making international travel less predictable and raising new risks for trade and cargo.

Earlier in September as part of "operation economic outcast," the US Treasury Department targeted Iran's aviation sector, including Iranian airlines and companies providing ground handling, ticketing or airport support, which face secondary sanctions and potentially lose access to the US financial system.

The United States cannot directly order foreign airports to reject Iranian aircraft. But the threat of secondary sanctions can make servicing them too risky for airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies.
For Tehran, the aviation sanctions are another layer of Washington's broader pressure campaign, alongside restrictions on banking, shipping, insurance and trade.
Washington argues that Iranian airlines have served not only civilian passengers but also military and security networks.
For example, Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and helping transport personnel and equipment.

The issue has also been debated inside Iran. Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said in a 2021 interview that Qassem Soleimani had used civilian aircraft to move forces and equipment to Syria.
For Washington, such links help justify targeting aviation networks. For ordinary travelers, however, the immediate result is canceled flights and fewer ways to leave or return to the country.
Major Middle East routes canceled

Iranian flights to Baghdad and Muscat have been suspended or canceled, while Azerbaijan and Georgia also stopped accepting flights operated by Iranian carriers. An Iranian travel agency told DW anonymously for safety reasons that routes to Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Georgia have been seriously disrupted.
On September 24, Turkmenistan refused permission for an Iranian aircraft flying from Tehran to Dushanbe to cross its airspace, forcing the plane to return to Iran.

Turkey, Armenia and China have not announced blanket restrictions, the agency said, but passengers were increasingly reluctant to buy tickets because even a confirmed booking did not guarantee departure.
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
A passenger told DW that agencies would still sell him a ticket but could not guarantee the flight would actually operate.

As part of the sanctions package, the US also suspended the "J-1" general license, which had allowed certain non-Iranian aircraft to make temporary stops in Iran under specific conditions, including that control of the aircraft remained with the foreign operator and that the stay did not exceed permitted limits.
Many commercial aircraft contain US-made parts or technology, meaning operations involving Iran can fall under US sanctions rules.

The suspension of J-1 has increased the legal and financial risks for airlines, airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling companies and other service providers, who now must calculate the risk of secondary sanctions.
More travelers use land crossings
With air connections increasingly uncertain, more passengers are turning to land crossings.
One traveler whose flight was canceled told DW that he traveled overland from Iran to Turkey before continuing to Istanbul by air.
"The border was very crowded. A lot of people were trying to leave because they were worried the routes might close," he told DW anonymously.

For families, elderly passengers, students and patients, however, crossing a land border and continuing by road and air can be far more difficult than taking a direct flight. Costs also rise quickly as passengers add road transport, accommodation and additional flights to journeys that previously required a single ticket.
Also affected is air freight, which is important for urgent or sensitive goods, including some medicines, medical equipment, industrial parts and laboratory samples.
That has become more significant as Iran simultaneously faces severe restrictions on maritime trade.
Iran's shaky aviation industry
Iranian aviation already faced structural problems before the latest sanctions.
Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh previously acknowledged that some flights operate without radar guidance, leaving pilots with greater responsibility for navigation.
An ageing fleet, difficulties obtaining spare parts, years of sanctions and fewer operational aircraft have all put pressure on airlines.
When passengers must also consider destination airports refusing services, lengthy delays or flights being canceled without warning, buying a ticket becomes a calculation of risk.

Alireza Salavati, political economy analyst and managing director of the London-based Middle East Analytica, said that the loss of air links will be unlikely to cause a large, immediate hit to Iran's GDP.

"Iran's aviation sector is small by regional standards. Unlike Turkey or the UAE, the country is not a major international hub, and its commercial fleet is limited. Officials said in July that roughly 150 aircraft were in the operational pool, with only about half of them operational at any given time," Salavati told DW.

"The damage is more apparent in connectivity. For a heavily sanctioned economy, flights still matter for business, the diaspora, students, specialist workers and medical treatment abroad. For patients, a once-direct journey can become a detour through a third country, with extra travel, accommodation and sometimes visa costs. Time can matter as much as money," Salavati added.
Iran offers plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days
Iran isolated by air and sea
Foreign airlines had already sharply reduced services to Iran before the latest measures.
Many passengers relied on Iranian carriers to reach regional hubs such as Istanbul, Muscat, Baghdad or Yerevan, then continued with foreign airlines.
If those first connections disappear, Iran's international aviation network could increasingly be reduced to a handful of routes that remain politically and commercially viable.

The development also comes as Iran faces restrictions at sea. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, higher insurance and freight costs and pressure on southern ports had already made imports and exports more difficult.
If maritime trade becomes more expensive while air links also contract, Iran will become increasingly dependent on land borders and indirect routes through neighboring states.
Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions?

articles.title: Plan for controversial Sydney data centre scrapped after push-back
articles.summary: Goodman Group, the property giant behind the Project Mars data centre, says the decision is due to changes to the "policy and regulatory environment".

blocks.text: Plans for a data centre which would have been built metres from people's homes in a Sydney suburb have been scrapped following intense push-back by campaigners.

The data centre was being developed by Goodman Group, Australia's biggest property company, and would have seen it construct a A$1.2bn (£630m; $841m), 90-megawatt facility known as Project Mars in the Lane Cove area.
The company confirmed it was withdrawing its application in a letter to the local planning authority. It follows a concerted opposition against the data centre by local residents and campaigners.
The dispute captures a wider disagreement in Australia over the role of data centres.

With the mainstreaming of generative AI in recent years, there has been a huge swell in demand for data centres, and Australia - with its abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land - has become a global destination for their construction.

However, while the country's government has been keen to attract investment from global AI companies, there has also been stiff opposition due to the huge demands the centres place on water and energy supplies, and the disruption they cause local communities.

The proposal for Project Mars, which would have been constructed about 20 metres from the nearest house in the suburb of Lane Cove, received 374 submissions during a consultation - with just nine in support of it.
According to local news website In the Cove, this is highest number of submissions ever received for a data centre application, external.

In its letter to New South Wales Department of Planning, Goodman Group said since starting the planning process in March 2025, it had "undertaken extensive technical investigations, stakeholder engagement and community consultation".
"During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly," it said.
It said it had "carefully considered these changes" along with the "views of the local community", and concluded it would not proceed with the development.
The decision by Goodman Group follows an announcement by the New South Wales government last month that it would be introducing a fast-track programme for data centres.
The programme would allow them to be assessed within 75 days, provided they meet requirements around certain standards and fund the additional supply of water and energy.

In a message posted to the Facebook page of Lane Cove Responsible Planning Group, Anthony Roberts, a member of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly representing Lane Cove, said it was "a huge win for the Lane Cove West community".
"This is a common-sense win for our community," he said.
"This victory sends a clear message to other data centre developers. To find suitable locations before putting proposals forward.
"Data centres have an important role to play, but developments of this size and scale need to be appropriately located and planned with the surrounding community in mind."

articles.title: Hungary lifts PM Peter Magyar’s immunity, clears way for probes into 2 former Orban ministers
articles.summary: Prime Minister Peter Magyar has backed the move himself. Two former ministers who served under his rival Viktor Orban now face separate corruption probes.

image.caption: Magyar, who attended parliament, has described the case against himself as a "farce"Image: Zsolt Szigetvary/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hungary's parliament on Monday lifted Prime Minister Peter Magyar's immunity from prosecution, along with that of two former ministers from Viktor Orban's government.
The votes clear the way for investigations involving Magyar and the two opposition lawmakers, who all face separate allegations.
What did the Hungarian lawmakers decide?

Parliament voted 139-0 to lift the immunity of Magyar, former Culture and Innovation Minister Balazs Hanko and former National Development Minister Miklos Sesztak. Lawmakers from Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party and its conservative Christian Democratic People's Party (KDNP) ally did not take part in the vote.
Magyar, whose center-right Tisza party came to power in April, had himself called on lawmakers to lift his immunity.
Prosecutors are investigating an incident in 2024 in which Magyar allegedly took a mobile phone from a man who was filming him at a Budapest nightclub and threw it into the Danube.
Hungary suspends 'Pro-Orban' public broadcasts
Magyar has described the case as a "farce" and accused prosecutors of trying to associate his case with corruption allegations against former members of Orban's government.
What are the former Orban ministers accused of?
Hanko, now a Fidesz lawmaker, is being investigated over the alleged misuse of public money from Hungary's National Cultural Fund.
Prosecutors allege that public funds were improperly used in more than 1,000 cases, causing losses of 17.3 billion forints (€44.5 million/$52.3 million). Hanko has rejected the allegations.

Sesztak, a KDNP lawmaker who served as national development minister from 2014 to 2018, faces a separate investigation concerning alleged bribes linked to contracts involving the state-owned bus company Volanbusz.
Magyar defeated Orban in April after campaigning on a pledge to investigate alleged corruption and abuses of power during Orban's 16 years in office.

articles.title: Israel does not have right to close UK consulate in Jerusalem, Foreign Office advised
articles.summary: Former attorney general Dominic Grieve says Israel is not entitled to shut mission in occupied Palestinian territory

blocks.text: Israel does not have a legal right to act on its plan to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, the former attorney general Dominic Grieve has advised the UK Foreign Office.
Israel has said it intends to shut the consulate on 8 October in response to the sweeping ban on trade with goods from Israeli settlements announced by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, this month.

Israel said on Sunday that it planned to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements.

Grieve, who was a Conservative MP between 1997 and 2019 and attorney general from 2010 to 2014, said Israel did not have the right to shut the consulate since it was situated in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.

When challenged in the Lords by the former UK ambassador Lord Hannay on the legality of Israel’s action, the Foreign Office minister Lord Wood said his fellow peer may have a point, and knew more about the subject than he did, but that he feared Israel de facto could make the consulate inoperable.
Grieve said the UK should challenge the decision in the courts, arguing Israel was asserting a right it did not possess as an occupying power to impose sovereign control over East Jerusalem.

blocks.caption: Dominic Grieve, who was attorney general under David Cameron. Photograph: Jacob King/PA

blocks.text: The UK mission in Jerusalem dates from 1838, predating the creation of the state of Israel by more than 100 years, and is separate from the embassy based in Tel Aviv. The consul general reports direct to the Foreign Office, and has its own staff and a distinct diplomatic role, covering Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza.

Grieve argues in an advisory paper sent to the Foreign Office by the British Palestine Project that “retaining a consulate general in East Jerusalem after recognition of the state of Palestine preserves the UK’s position that Jerusalem’s final status remains to be determined. It does not concede Israeli sovereignty.”

Grieve said the UK government had a duty to oppose the move. He pointed out the UK government had formally accepted the July 2024 advisory opinion of the international court of justice that governments should recognise Israel’s presence in occupied Palestinian territory as unlawful.

Separate from the legal position, Grieve said the closure of the consulate was a measure designed to fall on Palestinians, not on Britain alone, because it would hamper aid, oversight and reporting from the West Bank and Gaza.

He said: “Israel’s method in the city has been to create facts on the ground through unlawful settlement building and property seizure, and to press states to recognise those facts diplomatically. The closure should be challenged as a further attempt to exercise powers outwith those permitted to an occupier.”

In closing the consulate, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, asserted Israeli sovereignty over the whole city of Jerusalem, which the UN security council has expressly said Israel does not possess.
after newsletter promotion

The decision to revoke credentials of Dutch diplomats, announced by Sa’ar on Sunday, also in effect bars them from Israeli-controlled East Jerusalem and is likely to force the closure of their representative office in Ramallah.

The Netherlands’ ban on imports from occupied Palestine came into force on 22 September. The guidance applies to companies and individual travellers, and covers items bought before or after the legislation came into force, including gifts, souvenirs and items for personal use, the Dutch customs authority said.
Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine.

Sa’ar claimed that Dutch diplomats from the Ramallah mission could continue representing their nation’s interests “from Palestinian Authority territory, rather than from the territory of the state of Israel”. The Israeli foreign ministry did not immediately respond to questions about how this would work in practical terms.

When Israel took the same measures against Norwegian diplomats in 2024, in response to the country’s decision to recognise Palestine, it was forced to close its mission based in the West Bank town of al-Ram.

“We consider the Netanyahu government’s decision to be extreme and unreasonable,” the Norwegian foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said at the time. Diplomats based in Jordan have supported Norwegian relations with Palestine since then.

articles.title: Turkey: Comedian convicted for 'insulting' Erdogan in show
articles.summary: Deniz Goktas was convicted of two of three charges, including "insulting" the president, but was released pending the appeal process. Nominally, Turkey is a secular country with free speech.

image.caption: Goktas' show 'Dead Sea' gathered traction online in July, and shortly thereafer the comedian was detained on arrival at Istanbul's airport [Undated photo from the show]Image: YouTube/Deniz Göktaş

blocks.text: A Turkish comedian was convicted in Istanbul on Monday on charges of "insulting" President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and "insulting religious values" during a stand-up performance in June.
The judge provisionally sentenced Deniz Goktas to 19 months in prison, but ordered his release pending the judicial review and appeal process that would finalized the verdict.
It was not immediately clear how long this process might take.
NATO member and EU aspirant Turkey routinely tries people on speech-related offenses, particularly and famously when it comes to supposed "insults" of its longserving leader Erdogan.
What was the case about?

Deniz Goktas, 32, was arrested on July 3, a week after releasing a YouTube video of his show that was watched nearly 9 million times and a few days after shorter clips he posted on X enjoyed similar rapid success.
He faced an array of charges related to content in his "Dead Sea" show. Goktas referred to his impending court appointment online on Sunday, in one of his irreverent social media posts from his cell.

Goktas was accused of insulting Erdogan, of inciting public hatred and hostility — via jokes about Islam — and of praising crime and criminals, an additional charge added by prosecutors tied to a joke about an organized crime family, the Daltons

His trial is the latest in a widening crackdown on people seen as critical of Turkey's moderate Islamist government. Hundreds of politicians, artists, musicians, journalists and LGBTQ activists are among those to face detenion or trial.
LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown
What did Goktas say in his defense in court?
Goktas did not dispute the content from his popular show, but did argue in court that he had committed no crimes with his jokes.
Prosecutors had for instance singled out a pair of references he made to President Erdogan as a "dictator" as illegal insults.

"Dictator is not an insult: it is a political characterization," Goktas told the court. "As the president and leader of the party that has ruled the country for 25 years, a political comedy show in which Erdogan's name is never mentioned would be neither sincere nor have any connection to reality."
He said that Erdogan should be "open to the art of satire," as he said past presidents in Turkish democracy were.
"The joke hasn't changed. What has changed is the increasingly fragile leadership that can no longer tolerate the joke," he said.

The judge nevertheless convicted Gotkas of insulting Erdogan, and downgraded the charge he faced of "inciting hatred and hostility" with jokes about Islam, instead convicting him of the lesser supposed crime of "insulting religious values."
He cleared the comedian of the third charge of allegedly praising criminality.
Goktas has spent just under three months in pretrial detention, which should count as time served in any potential custodial sentence.

blocks.caption: News of Goktas' arrest in early July prompted protest in Istanbul [FILE: July 3, 2026]Image: Yasin Akgul/AFP

blocks.text: Erdogan the only claimant, Diyanet religious authority among those to complain
According to the Turkish NGO the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA), prosecutors cited more than 500 applications to prosecute the performer regarding the show.

They were issued to the Presidential Communication Center that monitors such issues. One of the groups to provide a tipoff was the government-sponsored Presidency of Religious affairs, better known as Diyanet.
Erdogan, in charge of Turkey either as prime minister or later president since 2003, was named as the sole complainant.

His government has attracted attention in recent years for its prosecution of people deemed to have unfairly criticized the authorities, and for the various lawsuits against leading members of the opposition, particularly the CHP. The Turkish president's litigious streak also became headline news in Germany around a decade ago, when he pursued star TV comedian Jan Böhmermann.

Meanwhile the MLSA said that Goktas' jokes alleged to have the potential to "publicly incite hatred and hostility" took aim at fundamentalist Islam, including a reference to women in full-coverage swimsuits being "divers" and joking about "suicide bombers who fast."
Turkey nominally has a secular constitution and guarantees of free speech. However, the EU and the US have often criticized its application of these standards.

The US Commission on International Religious Freedom wrote in a 2022 report that Erdogan's government increasingly relied on speech-based prosecution to "silence individuals who express criticism in religious terms, disclose beliefs or a lack thereof that differ from those of the majority of the population, or engage with religion in a way perceived as 'mocking' or 'irreverent.'"

articles.title: Three people dead, including a child, in attempt to cross Channel to UK
articles.summary:
Dozens also reported injured after inflatable boat carrying 105 people gets into trouble off northern France

A child was among three people who died ⁠and dozens of others who were injured…

blocks.text: A child was among three people who died ⁠and dozens of others who were injured while ⁠attempting ​to cross the Channel on Monday, French authorities have said.
France’s maritime ​police ‌said ‌it received a ‌distress call in the early hours from an inflatable dinghy carrying 105 people that had ‌run into trouble in calm seas.

The vessel had reportedly overturned, killing a 10-year-old and two women. The three passengers were treated on board but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter.
The incident happened off the coast of Wissant, a village in northern France’s Pas-de-Calais department.
A spokesperson for the local prefecture confirmed “a provisional total of three deaths and many more injured”, adding that “sea conditions were calm – the weather is good”.
The prefecture described the boat as a “water taxi”, saying it had arrived relatively empty from an inland waterway before picking up passengers from the beach at Wissant.
At 10.30am local time – 9.30am, UK time – six rescue boats were still at the scene searching for people in the water.

At least 17 people, including women and children, have died in the Channel this year while attempting to reach the UK. Many have drowned, while others have died in incidents involving overcrowded boats.
Three bodies were found last week after chaotic “water taxi” departures of this kind in northern France.

So far this year, 18,609 people have made the Channel crossing – more than 40 per cent fewer than at the same point last year. The number is also more than 25 per cent lower than at this stage in 2024, when 25,165 people had crossed the Channel.
Last week also saw two uncontrolled landings in the UK, where dinghies arrived without being intercepted by authorities.
It comes as more than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died while attempting to reach Spain’s Canary Islands by sea in August.

On Monday, a rescue boat arrived at the port of Calais in the mid-morning, where it began disembarking people rescued from the accident. A coach, fire service and police vehicles were deployed at the scene.
The northern beaches of France have become a key crossing point for people without visas hoping to cross the Channel.
They pay people smugglers to board unstable rubber dinghies to make the journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.
At least 29 people lost their lives last year trying to cross the Channel, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official French and British sources.
Official figures cited by the UN refugee agency, the UNHCR, show irregular migration to the EU – notably via Mediterranean sea routes – has plummeted since its peak during the 2015 refugee crisis.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will on Monday announce the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees in the UK as she says “fairness” is at the heart of her vision for the Home Office.
It will come as she focuses on safe and legal refugee routes to the UK in her Labour party conference speech.
The UK resettlement scheme will reopen immediately, with around a quarter of those admitted to the UK under it expected to be Palestinians and women and girls from Afghanistan.
UK government sources said officials were aware of the fatalities.

articles.title: Diesel prices are surging putting further pressure on Europe
articles.summary: Trucks, farms and industry are powered with diesel. Now prices are soaring due to refinery disruptions, supply shortages and geopolitical tensions. A potential US export ban could make Europe's…

image.caption: Global diesel refining capacity has become so tight that every disruption has an outsized impact on availability and pricesImage: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: Even if you don't fill your own vehicle with diesel, its price has a big impact on your life.
While gasoline is mainly a consumer fuel for cars, diesel powers much of the wider economy, from freight transport and farming equipment to construction and industry.
That is why diesel shortages or price shocks can have a bigger economic impact than higher gasoline prices by raising the cost of moving goods and operating heavy machinery.
As businesses become strained, these higher energy costs will be passed on to consumers and add to a growing cost-of-living crisis and inflation. So what's driving global diesel prices higher?
The US blames Ukraine for diesel shortages
The United States and China are among the world's largest diesel producers. China keeps much of it for domestic use, leaving the US as the world's biggest diesel exporter.

Still, the weekly average price of a gallon of diesel is now $6.52 (€5.73) in the country, according to the US Energy Information Administration, a big increase from a year ago when it averaged $3.74 per gallon or two years ago when it averaged $3.53 a gallon.
President Donald Trump recently called on Ukraine's president to stop targeting oil refineries in Russia "because he's causing a shortage of diesel."
Russia is one of the world's other biggest diesel suppliers. But since 2022, some of its oilrefineries have been attacked as many as 15 times, according to the International Energy Agency.
The agency estimates that diesel production in Russia is down by nearly 30% from 2025 levels. Moscow has now restricted diesel exports to protect domestic supplies.

blocks.caption: While petrol is primarily a consumer fuel for cars, diesel is important to the wider economy and just-in-time deliveryImage: Viacheslav Madiievskyi/Ukrinform/ABACA/picture alliance

blocks.text: As Russian production declined, the US went into high gear to help make up the difference, but even this was not enough. And on September 22, Trump announced that his administration was also considering a diesel export ban.
Such a move is likely an attempt to bring down domestic prices ahead of the November midterm elections since energy prices and affordability have become important campaign issues.

Leading energy lobby groups have come out against such a plan, and many industry experts think a ban would be slow to bring down prices or could backfire by pushing US refiners to reduce production, push up prices, or both.
Europe is especially vulnerable to diesel shocks
For Europe, more expensive diesel could have dramatic consequences.

"Decades of policy incentives, such as tax advantages, left Europe's vehicle fleet far more diesel-heavy than regions like the US," said Georg Zachmann, a senior fellow at Brussels-based Bruegel think tank.
"As a result, the EU is structurally long on gasoline, which it exports, and short on diesel, which it must import," added Zachmann, who specializes in energy and climate policies.

In the EU, just over 38% of passenger cars are diesel and road transport, including freight, makes up 77% of total diesel and gas oil consumption, according to a briefing published by Transport & Environment, a Brussels-based advocacy group.
This reliance on diesel-powered transport "leaves drivers and businesses particularly exposed to oil and fuel price shocks," wrote Juliette Egal, the briefing's lead author.

The NGO calculated that EU drivers are paying €30 more for a 50-liter tank of diesel on average since the start of the war in Iran. An average German long-haul truck driver is paying an extra €236 a week.

Increased fuel costs for EU road transport add up to €270 million a day — of that, €203 million is for diesel, according to the briefing. Overall, the EU economy has seen additional costs of €40 billion from road diesel since the beginning of the war.
Why are diesel prices climbing faster than oil?
In the near term, Russia's crude oil processing volumes are the single fastest-moving lever, said Skip York, a nonresident fellow at Rice University's Center for Energy Studies in Houston, Texas.
"Each new wave of Ukrainian strikes shows up in diesel prices within days, unlike Hormuz, which has been running at a depressed but relatively stable flow rate for months," he added.
Why Iran fuel crisis hits different in Europe than the US

York points out that, perhaps surprisingly, crude oil production, the raw material needed to make diesel and gasoline, isn't the biggest constraint. That is why oil prices have moved modestly while diesel has soared.
"The oil bottleneck has shifted from 'not enough crude' in March/April to 'not enough refining capacity' since August," the expert told DW.
Now refinery disruptions matter most, he said, because "both the Ukraine drone campaign and the Hormuz conflict are knocking out working refining capacity faster than anyone can replace it."
Still, the Strait of Hormuz "is the bigger structural risk" for diesel prices in the long term.
Globally, refinery capacity has "dropped substantially, and diesel is particularly affected," agreed Zachmann.
Where will diesel prices go from here?
Prolonged fighting in the Middle East or Russia could add to the problems for Europe and other diesel users. US export restrictions could make this situation even worse.

US diesel exports to Europe are up around 37% since last year and now account for about 8% of European demand, says York. This makes the country an important alternative to diesel from Russia and the Persian Gulf.

If the US blocks exports, it would be a big shock and mean even higher diesel prices, said Zachmann. The question is whether the EU would retaliate and export less gasoline to the US "making both sides worse off" by pushing up both US gasoline prices and EU diesel prices.
Is Europe prepared for its next major energy shock?
Additionally, winter is just around the corner for the Northern Hemisphere. Refineries may struggle to meet demand for both heating oil and diesel, further tightening supplies.
A wave of refinery closures in Europe and the US since 2019 has made the diesel market vulnerable, said York, and this has hit the buffer of spare refining capacity that used to absorb shocks.
"Essentially, the market has fewer 'extra barrels' standing by," he underscored. "So, the loss of any barrel hits supply much more directly than it used to."

articles.title: Iran says it ‘has no plans to negotiate with US’ despite Trump claims – US politics live
articles.summary:
Trump had told Axios he expected talks to resume a day after he rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

State…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 6m agoIran has 'no plans to negotiate with US' despite Trump claims in media

blocks.text: Iran has 'no plans to negotiate with US' despite Trump claims in media
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
State media in Iran has reported that Iran’s delegation to the UN General Assembly had no talks planned with the United States, after US president Donald Trump said he expected more negotiations.
“Iran’s delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States,” said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group.
Trump told media outlet Axios on Sunday that he expected talks to resume soon, a day after he rejected a proposal by Tehran to reopen the strait of Hormuz within seven days.
“Iran’s views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the US side... via a Qatari mediator,” IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday.
Iran says it presented seven conditions for ending the war and reopening the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which roughly 20% of the world’s oil and gas flowed before the war.

The strait lies at the heart of the conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Following that attack, Tehran placed a chokehold on the waterway, and Washington responded with a blockade of Iranian ports.

Axios said indirect talks mediated by Qatar could take place as early as today, less than a week after similar discussions between US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi.
Iran demands a seven-day ceasefire across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, where its ally Hezbollah is regularly bombarded by Israel.
It also demands the unfreezing of its foreign assets, lifting sanctions on its oil sector, and an end to the US naval blockade. Trump rejected their demands on Saturday.
In other developments:

items: The Trump administration on Monday plans to release new fuel economy standards that would relax regulatory requirements for automakers to control pollution from gasoline-powered cars and light trucks. President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social media account on Saturday that the less stringent mileage requirements would “take the waste out of building cars in America” and save families “thousands on a new, beautiful and safe car,” while boosting auto production in the US.

Donald Trump’s attorney general Todd Blanche argued on Sunday that the administration was permitted to ban three news outlets from the White House because “it is a privilege and not a right to be there”. Appearing on the ABC News program This Week during the second week of the White House’s dispute over press credentialing and access, Blanche also said that the administration took the decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico beginning on 19 September because the president was “sick and tired” of what he considered to be those media outlets’ inaccurate reporting.

US senator Thom Tillis on Sunday criticized Donald Trump, his fellow Republican, for the president’s support of Ken Paxton over incumbent John Cornyn in the Texas Senate Republican primary. “He made a colossal mistake,” Tillis, a frequent Trump critic from North Carolina, said during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union in reference to the president’s support of Paxton who defeated Cornyn in the May primary.

The United States and China released Monday reciprocal lists of products worth about $30bn each that will see tariff cuts, in a deal expected to boost bilateral trade. The details came days after Chinese President Xi Jinping met with president Donald Trump in Washington in his first state visit to the US since 2015.

Trump justified the pending US arms sale to Taiwan to Chinese president Xi Jinping by downplaying it as just one of many sales Washington makes around the world - even asking Xi if he’d be in the market for US arms, Trump’s ambassador to China said on Sunday.

House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda, with investigations of Trump, his family and his administration if the party sweeps control of the chamber from Republicans in the November elections. The undertaking is as robust as it is daunting, spanning several House committees.

articles.title: Hurricane Polo threatens Mexico's Pacific coast with landfall expected today
articles.summary: Residents of Mexico's Baja California Sur state boarded up homes and workers hauled dirt and rubble to shore up embankments as Hurricane Polo bore down on the peninsula Monday, threatening high…

image.caption: Workers pull a boat to shore Monday ahead of the arrival of Hurricane Polo in Puerto San Carlos, Mexico. (Eduardo Verdugo/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Residents of Mexico's Baja California Sur state boarded up homes and workers hauled dirt and rubble to shore up embankments as Hurricane Polo bore down on the peninsula Monday, threatening high winds, floods and mudslides. Meanwhile, Hurricane Nolo could still bring torrential rain to parts of Hawaii even as the storm edged away from the state.
Hurricane Nolo moving away from Hawaii, but could still bring torrential rain

In Puerto San Carlos, Mexico, a fishing town of about 5,700 people, some feared high tides and pounding waves from Polo could breach barriers and send seawater into the community. Some families planned to head to shelters in Ciudad Constitucion, about 60 kilometres away, while dozens of people elsewhere in the state were evacuated.

"Civil Protection told those of us here in San Carlos to evacuate because this is a high-risk area. With the current tides, the expected waves and the wind, the earthen barriers they built [to prevent flooding] could give way," said fisherwoman Rocío Sánchez.
Rains, winds, floods
Polo was a Category 3 storm with top sustained winds of 185 km/h on Monday morning, the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said.

Forecasters said it would hit the Mexican mainland after lashing Baja California Sur with heavy rains, and that "life threatening winds and flash floods" were expected to occur soon. It could bring heavy rain and flooding to parts of the U.S. Southwest later in the week.

"Polo is forecast to be near major hurricane strength when it reaches Baja California Sur later today, and is anticipated to be a hurricane when it makes landfall in mainland Mexico late tonight or early Tuesday morning," the centre said.

By Monday morning, waves began to crash and flood coastal areas. Laura Velázquez, national co-ordinator of Mexico's Civil Protection Agency, reported that Polo would make landfall later in the afternoon.

At a Monday morning news briefing, she urged residents to stay off the streets and seek shelter if their homes are at risk. She said travel will be suspended in the area where the hurricane was expected to make landfall and that ports across the region would be closed.

Nolo, meanwhile, was well southwest of Hawaii and moving away from the Big Island as the weekend drew to a close, but a wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Monday morning. Nolo's maximum sustained winds increased to near 249 km/h.

Storm activity in the Pacific has been above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season, according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec. He said that pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.

With Polo approaching Mexico, the Mexican navy said it has gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlan on the Pacific Coast, and deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the storm.

One of the towns in the hurricane's projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja's Pacific coast. The town has only had full-time electricity for a few years, and still experiences frequent outages. There is concern that washed-out roads could block access to medical facilities.
"Our people are concerned about this event," said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel. "We haven't faced such a worrying situation in many years."
Robles Meza said Sunday that army soldiers arrived in San Juanico to prepare a shelter and provide support for possible emergencies.

Also Sunday, Tropical Storm Rachel formed well off Mexico's southwest coast. The hurricane centre said Monday that Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 85 km/h and was located about 365 kilometres south-southwest of Acapulco. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect.
Floods and mudslides still a risk in Hawaii

Forecasters said Nolo's outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 50 centimetres of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands.

More than 120 U.S. National Guard members were activated, part of roughly 400 statewide after the governor issued an emergency proclamation. U.S. President Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to co-ordinate assistance and provide funding support.
Power outages persist on Maui, with over 10,000 households and businesses primarily on the west side of the island lacking electricity Monday morning, according to poweroutage.us.

Most of the outages were related to storm damage, according to statements from Hawaiian Electric. High winds of over 96 km/h Sunday prevented helicopters from flying over mountain ridges this weekend to assess transmission line damage, the utility said, adding that it expected the outages to persist until midday Monday.

The utility this weekend also de-energized lines around a brush fire that broke out Saturday, prompting evacuation orders several kilometres south of Lahaina, the site of the 2023 deadly fires. Those evacuation orders were lifted Monday morning.
Hawaii's residents are still recovering from Hurricane Lala, which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.

articles.title: Will Jürgen Klopp's charisma be enough for Germany?
articles.summary: After defeat to Greece, Jürgen Klopp is confronted with the real challenge of his task as Germany head coach. Can his charisma alone push this group forward?

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp has a lot of work to do, but is his charisma alone enough to carry this Germany team?Image: Steffie Wunderl/BEAUTIFUL SPORTS/picture alliance

blocks.text: In his first season in charge at Liverpool, Jürgen Klopp lost just one of his first five games. Germany are hoping for a similar run emerges after a shock defeat to Greece left Klopp with just one point after his first two games.
Klopp's response was familiar. The head coach took responsibility for the loss, shielding this new crop of Germany players from criticism.
"We have been together for a week now, all mixed together, and that needs time," Klopp said after the match.

"Let the new players develop. The established players are top players at their clubs, and they have my support. Feel free to criticize me, but not the boys. We don't need to completely tear everything apart. I was surprised that some people booed. The future is as bright as we make it. We'll take it on with everything we have."
He also emphasized development over short-term panic, citing the need for more training sessions to cement the automatic responses needed to break down well-organized defenses.
International coaching is different

Herein lies the challenge for one of football's greatest coaches. In likely his final job as a head coach, can the multiple league winner adapt his coaching methods to work in the international setting? Klopp, a coach and a person famous for his ability to develop relationships and grow a team at a club, has said he believes he can adapt.

There is no doubt his communication style is what this team needs. His charismatic focus on developing a culture and growing collectively in connection with the fans is what is required. And after many years of frustration and pain watching Germany's men at major tournaments, the biggest mistake would be to tear down this new group before it even begins.

It both needs and deserves the time to figure out how far it can go. Bambase Conte and Hennes Behrens made their debuts vs. Greece after a host of others had done so against the Netherlands. These are the first steps towards finding out who will drive Germany towards an improved outing at Euro 2028 in two summer's time. It is the main reason why Klopp chose so many players for these first four games.
Can Klopp alone compensate should ability be lacking?

But what if, for all of Klopp's positivity and culture building, this new generation of Germany players is just not good enough to win a trophy? Clearly, it is too soon to know the answer to that question, as Klopp himself has said.
"We want to help prepare these players to be competing at the very top over the next two or three years," Klopp had said at his unveiling.
"We took a different approach and focused not on what we don't have, but on what we do have."
What Germany do have right now is both a new team looking to grow and a team that just suffered their first-ever defeat to Greece.

At Liverpool, it took Jürgen Klopp two years and approximately 500 odd training sessions, to reach the point where the team looked like his. In the 2017-18 season, they reached the Champions League final. Alongside the time it took for the team to learn the new system, new signings, notably Mo Salah, Roberto Firmino and Sadio Mane, improved the quality.

Klopp doesn't have that option in the Germany job. He has to do more with fewer training sessions – Klopp will have approximately 200 before Euro 2028. And the closest he can get to new signings are by calling up uncapped Germany players – there were 11 first-time call-ups in this Germany squad.
The 59-year-old said his whole career brought him to this job. It might well prove to be the greatest challenge of his career too.

articles.title: Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in Nations League match overshadowed by political controversy
articles.summary: Ireland easily beat Israel in a Nations League fixture that 24 hours earlier appeared in doubt. One Irish player pulled out of the match to express his opposition to Israel's actions in the Gaza…

image.caption: Members of the Irish team bowed their heads during playing of the Israeli national anthemImage: Inpho Photography/IMAGO

blocks.text: The Irish team bowed their heads during playing of the Israeli national anthem on Sunday night and they declined to shake hands with their opponents, a gesture that is customary before international fixtures.

Ireland played the match wearing black armbands in memory of those killed in Israel's military operation in the Gaza Strip, and just 24 hours earlier it was unclear whether the match would go ahead at all.
'Significant majority' vote to play
On Saturday, the players voted in favor of playing what was technically a home match for Israel in Debrecen, Hungary, despite widespread opposition to their participation among the Irish public.

David Courell, the chief executive of the Irish FA (FAI), told a press conference that had been delayed for several hours while players and coaches met to discuss the issue, that a significant majority of the squad had voted to play.
"Based on that, the association took ⁠the decision on behalf of Irish ​football that this fixture would continue, as we have always intended to fulfil the fixtures," he said.
However, the vote was not unanimous and one player, reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, decided to pull out of the squad for this and a second match against Israel during this international break.
In Sunday's match, Troy Parrott netted the opener for Ireland in the 14th minute, with ​Adam Idah scoring two minutes later. Jack Moylan added a third in the 25th to make the final score 3-0.

blocks.caption: Troy Parrott opened the scoring for IrelandImage: Inpho Photography/IMAGO

blocks.text: Few supporters present
The fixture was played in a largely empty stadium in Debrecen, with just a few hundred Israeli fans and a handful of Irish supporters in attendance.
The FAI had not reserved any tickets for their fans to attend the match and public broadcaster RTE showed the match without the usual halftime analysis.
Over the previous few days, the Irish team had been under intense pressure from Irish fans and politicians to boycott the fixture.

Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause and formally recognized a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway. Dublin has also repeatedly criticized Israel over the Gaza conflict.
A Hamas raid into Israel on October 7, 2023, killed around 1,200 people, prompting Israel's attack on Gaza which has killed over 73,000.

Ireland's next Nations League match was originally scheduled to be played in Dublin on October 4, but due to security concerns, it has been moved to the Serbian town of Backa Topola, where it is to be played behind closed doors.

articles.title: Sweden faces political deadlock after election-winning center-left bloc fails to form government
articles.summary: Swedish Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson has abandoned efforts to form a four-party government. Deep divisions within the election-winning bloc have left Sweden in political…

image.caption: The collapse of Andersson's government talks gives Sweden's outgoing right-wing bloc a chance to try to remain in powerImage: Jonas Ekströmer/TT NEWS AGENCY/picture alliance

blocks.text: The leader of Sweden's center-left Social Democratic Party, Magdalena Andersson, on Monday said her talks with other parties had failed to form a government after her bloc's narrow election victory.
The breakdown leaves Sweden without a new government more than two weeks after the election and opens the door for the outgoing right-wing bloc to try to remain in power despite losing the vote.
Why did Sweden's government talks fail?
Andersson had been trying to bring together the Social Democrats, Greens, Center Party and Left Party, which together won 176 of parliament's 349 seats.
But talks foundered on deep divisions between the centrist Center Party and socialist Left Party.
"Based on the discussions I have had, I can conclude that, as things currently stand, it is not possible for me to form a government," Andersson told reporters.
The four-party bloc won 176 seats in the September 13 election, compared with 173 for the outgoing right-wing alliance. The popular vote difference was around 50,000.
What happens next?

The speaker of parliament is now expected to ask another party leader to try to form a government, with outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson of the center-right Moderate Party the likely next choice.
How Sweden's tough migration policy impacts youth

Kristersson continues to lead a caretaker government. His bloc, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats, has also failed to secure a majority and would probably need support from the Center Party.
Center Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist has ruled out supporting a government that gives influence to either the Sweden Democrats or the Left Party.
Protracted government formation is not unusual in Sweden. It took 37 days to establish a government following the 2022 election and 134 days after the vote in 2018.

articles.title: Thai downpours shift north-westwards after Bangkok declared a disaster zone
articles.summary:
Capital city submerged in waist-high flood water, while elsewhere Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii’s Big Island

Bangkok was

blocks.text: Bangkok was declared a disaster zone by its city officials towards the end of last week, after streets in Thailand’s capital city were submerged in up to waist-high flood water. The flooding stemmed from an active cell of low pressure across central Thailand that brought continuous heavy rainfall and thunderstorms to Bangkok and surrounding regions.

The heavy rain began early on Thursday when the weak area of low pressure travelled north-westwards up the gulf of Thailand before then sitting over central Thailand by Friday morning. For most of the following two days this low pressure remained roughly in situ, which allowed unrelenting downpours over Bangkok and nearby areas. One weather station near Prachin Buri, just north-east of the capital, recorded 213.5mm within a 24-hour period between Friday and Saturday evening local time – for comparison, London receives an average 585mm a year). Fortunately, the centre of the low-pressure cell shifted north-westwards on Sunday and brought an end to the torrential rainfall.

Out in the central Pacific, meanwhile, citizens of Hawaii’s Big Island were threatened by Hurricane Nolo over the weekend. The system initially approached the archipelago early last week, bringing heavy rainfall from around Tuesday evening. By the early hours of Saturday Nolo was a category 2 hurricane, with sustained windspeeds of 85-90knots (98-104mph), situated at its closest to the archipelago at approximately 145 miles (233km) south of the Big Island. Strong winds were not the only threat to the Big Island, as the vast quantity of rainfall raised concerns over flooding and mudslides. Since the impacts of Nolo started late on Tuesday 22 September, weather stations in the north-east of the island have received over 530mm of rainfall. Fortunately, Nolo has propagated westwards away from Hawaii where it is forecast to peak in its intensity on Monday 28 September, with current predictions of achieving category 4 status.
after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, farther east in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is now forecast to make landfall with the Baja California peninsula late in the day on Monday 28 September. The once category 5 hurricane will downgrade to category 2 by landfall with sustained winds of 96-110mph. A hurricane warning has been issued in coastal regions due to the risk of a storm surge where winds are onshore. Polo will also bring intense downpours while traversing the peninsula with 100-200mm expected, potentially reaching up to 250mm locally. The bulk of this rain falling within a 12-hour period and bringing the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. The storm will continue to weaken while propagating north-eastwards across the Sonora region in Mexico.

blocks.text: Live

A university in Punjab has suspended classes after protests over a rumored sexual assault took a violent turn. Separately, the Supreme Court has taken suo motu cognizance of recent rape cases in Delhi. DW has more.

blocks.caption: Over 2,000 police personnel were deployed to ensure security on the campusImage: ANI

blocks.text: What you need to know
These are our rolling updates from India on Monday, September 28:

items: Lovely Professional University in Punjab suspends classes for 10 days after protests that erupted over claims of a campus rape ended in clashes
The Supreme Court of India says increasing rape cases in Delhi and the National Capital Region 'underline a systemic failure' by law enforcement and administration

blocks.text: Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
September 28, 2026
Lovely Professional University protest: Classes suspended after violence during protests over suspected assault

Punjab's Lovely Professional University (LPU) has suspended classes starting Monday and postponed mid-term examinations after a protest over an alleged rape turned violent on Sunday with protesters clashing with the police and vandalism being reported.

The private university located in the city of Phagwara witnessed massive student unrest after claims spread on social media that a female university student was allegedly raped within the campus premises by an outsider and had later died by suicide.

The protests grew to be violent when the protesters clashed with the police, pelted stones at the security personnel, smashed windows and set fire to some objects within the university complex, reports said.
Some students later claimed in social media posts that the vandals were not students, but outsiders.
Heavy police deployment
The university has suspended regular classes for 10 days, news agency ANI cited a statement from LPU as saying.

The statement said students could travel to their hometowns during the suspension of classes and advised those who stay back to remain in their hostels or places of accommodation and avoid any unnecessary movement. The statement also called on students to avoid involvement in the unrest.
Over 2,000 police personnel were deployed to ensure security on the campus, reports quoted the Additional Director General of Police Fayaz Farooqui as saying.
The protesters also blocked the national highway between Jalandhar and Phagwara highway early Sunday, leading to traffic disruptions.
On Monday, police said that the situation had been brought under control and traffic movement on the highway had been restored.
Claims of rape remain unverified
Meanwhile, the police are yet to confirm whether a student was raped within LPU's campus. They have launched an investigation to examine the facts of the incident.
Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann has taken note of the situation and has directed the Director General of Police to visit the campus, reports said on Monday.
Meanwhile, the Punjab State Women Commision is seeking a detailed report on the alleged rape, ANi reported.
What has LPU said?
The LPU has denied that the alleged rape took place, calling the claims "false, baseless and fabricated rumors".
The university on Sunday posted a video with three female students who it said reside in the girls' hostel room where the alleged incident is claimed to have taken place.
The video purportedly shows the girls denying that there had been a rape, with one of them asking the police to stop visiting the room repeatedly.

However, media reports on Monday said that the same girls later appear in a separate purported video, claiming that they were instructed on what to say in the statement. They then allegedly claim that their clips were "trimmed" and used without their consent.

articles.title: 'Thrown under the bus': Former defence chief's memoir lays bare his battles with the Trudeau government
articles.summary: Former defence chief Wayne Eyre considered quitting "several times" as he battled the Trudeau government over military misconduct, defence spending and support for Ukraine. His candid memoir recounts…

image.caption: Prime Minister Justin Trudeau shakes hands with Gen. Wayne Eyre, outgoing Chief of the Defence Staff, after his remarks at a change of command ceremony in Ottawa on July 18, 2024. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada's former top military commander considered resigning "several times" during his tenure in battles with the former Trudeau government over the sexual misconduct scandal, and the lack of commitment towards defence spending.

Retired general Wayne Eyre's new memoir, Into the Breach: A Soldier's Journey, also peels back the curtain on the internal debate that took place over how to end the convoy occupation of downtown Ottawa in early 2022.
The prologue to the book, titled The Accidental CDS, is a tongue-in-cheek reference to his unusual, unexpected rise to the position of chief of the defence staff.

Eyre was promoted from being army commander to the top job after now-retired admiral Art MacDonald stepped aside in February 2021 because of allegations of inappropriate behaviour. Those allegations never resulted in charges and MacDonald didn't return to the defence chief's job.
Eyre was left to navigate the wider sexual misconduct scandal and a flurry of allegations which engulfed several high-ranking military leaders — an experience he described as "soul crushing."
He candidly writes about how, in the first few months, he often questioned whether he was up to the task.
Eyre's memoir recounts a highly charged incident in June 2021 where he said he felt thrown "under the bus" by former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland.

At the time, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Freeland both publicly questioned Eyre's decision to allow the now-former commander of the navy, Vice-Admiral Craig Baines, to remain in his post after he took part in a golf game with former chief of the defence staff Jonathan Vance, who had been under military police investigation following allegations of inappropriate behaviour.
In Eyre's view, Freeland's criticism amounted to forcing the prime minister to choose between his deputy and his senior military adviser.

"If there's no trust between the nation's senior military leader and the nation's senior elected leader, one of them has to go, and it's not going to be the elected leader," Eyre said in an interview with CBC News.
Support from Trudeau kept him from resigning

The incident culminated, Eyre said, when he was on the phone with the prime minister to discuss the decision to retain Baines. He was just about to resign when Trudeau stopped him by saying he still had confidence in him.

After his initial criticism, the prime minister made a further statement of support for his defence chief — remarks Eyre had not seen when the phone call was placed. The crisis was defused, but the tension remained.
Former military commander Eyre says he thought about resigning 'several times'
Eyre served another three years after the incident.
Resignation crossed his mind "several times" as internal battles unfolded over defence funding and the deteriorating state of readiness in the military.
Ultimately, he decided to stay because quitting would have precipitated a further crisis in an already wounded institution.
"You've got to be very careful as a military leader about resigning. You can fall on your sword, but generally it hurts and you can only do it once," he said.

"Resigning is an inherently political act, which could further fray political-military relations, [and] would cause a momentary blip in the media cycle. But at the same time, [it would] cause significant turmoil in the institution."

items: Gen. Wayne Eyre stepping down from position as Canada's top military commander

blocks.text: Throughout his tenure there was a series of rolling crises including the various waves of the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 11, 2022.
At the time, the Trudeau government faced public criticism about its reluctance to approve lethal aid for the embattled Eastern European country. It was a struggle, Eyre acknowledged.
"What we experienced at that time was a collision of ideology with reality," he told CBC.
"The ideology being, we are Canada, we don't supply weapons to a conflict zone. The reality was, OK, this is coming, Ukraine is a friend, this [is] one way we can help."
'Lethargy to approve a new defence policy'

Eyre's book is littered with further examples related to Canada's mission to train Ukraine troops and the transfer of M-777 artillery, underlining his frustration with the government's seeming "inability to make decisions at the speed of war."
He did note there were times when Canada later outstripped its allies in the swift delivery of war supplies and equipment, such as Leopard tanks.
The overall sense of frustration came into sharp focus during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's September 2023 visit to Canada, which included a series of speeches in Toronto.

items: Zelenskyy's 1st visit to Canada since Russia's war 'emotional,' say some Ukrainians

blocks.text: "Both the PM and Deputy PM Freeland gave bellicose, impassioned speeches about being strong and supporting Ukraine," Eyre wrote, noting the contradiction between the political rhetoric and the fiscal reality that faced the Canadian military at the time.

"I, like the handful of CAF senior leaders present, had a hard time reconciling these otherwise great speeches with both the billion-dollar budget cut that they had just inflicted on us and their lethargy to approve a new defence policy."
The deeper the war in Ukraine became, the more concerned Eyre became about the state of Canada's readiness.
‘Urgency is required,’ says outgoing chief of defence staff Gen. Wayne Eyre on Russia-Ukraine war

He described how, in June 2022, during the run-up to the unveiling of Canada's new policy commitment to NORAD — the by national aerospace command — no one seemed to know where $38 billion in funding was going to come from, or where it would be allocated.

"Most galling was the 'smoke and mirrors' funding approach, with billions already allocated for other military equipment taken away and reallocated, with most investments only coming years into the future," Eyre wrote.
"With confusion persisting several days later, I drew some government ire when I frankly told a journalist that the source of funds 'wasn’t clear to me.'"

items: Top soldier says military looking for 'clarity' on Ottawa's budget plans

blocks.text: Military 'compartmentalized' Ottawa convoy involvement
The memoir also sheds light on a passing reference that appeared in the public hearings related to the invocation of the Emergencies Act to end the convoy protest.

Former deputy defence minister Bill Matthews testified that the military prepared operational plans as a precaution, but they were dismissed due to significant concerns that deploying troops would escalate tensions and mirror the 1990 Oka Crisis.

Throughout the convoy protest crisis, Eyre was firmly opposed to the notion that the military had any sort of role whatsoever. He attempted to correct the public perception by saying there's a difference between planning and scenario spinning.
"We looked at various scenarios, and it wasn't planning because a plan entails assigning troops to task and warning at all levels and the like," Eyre told CBC News.

"No, it was more thinking about various scenarios, and what questions would we have to ask, what measures would have to be taken. But given the sensitivity at the time, it was very compartmentalized."
Most of the discussion, he said, revolved around the use of military tow-trucks to remove protest vehicles.
In his memoir, Eyre wrote: "At the time one of my staff commented, 'If you accomplish nothing else as CDS, keeping the CAF out of this mess is a singular achievement.'"
Canada 'on the right path,' Eyre says
During his final months as defence chief and in his departure speech, Eyre warned about how dangerous the world had become and how Canada needed to prepare.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government reversed many Trudeau-era policies and has begun substantially investing in defence — taking the country to the NATO standard of two per cent of the gross domestic product.

Several European political leaders, as well as security and intelligence agencies have warned that the West is likely to face a major conflict with Russia and possibly even China by the end of the decade.
Asked by CBC whether he thought the country was ready for what may be coming in the next few years, Eyre said no.
"But we're on the right path, and we are getting there."

articles.title: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most
articles.summary: The most revealing thing about the summit in Washington may be what the two leaders did not say - and what we still don't know.

blocks.text: Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January.
The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year.
Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December.
It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently.
But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough.
China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing.
Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs.
The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028.
What is striking is what was left out.
There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased.
The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping.
According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution.
After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack.
He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue.
This time, Trump disclosed far less.
"We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend.
"Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel."
That silence may be significant.
Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months.
Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit.
The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so.

Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations.
The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it.

Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed.
Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen.
And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans.

Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention.
So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place.
